name: Hana Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Martin and I farm Highcroft, which has been in his family four generations. We've a hundred and twenty breeding ewes, twenty suckler cows, and we grow oats and cut hay for the winter on the lower fields. I'm up at six, feed the dogs, then out to the stock, and in summer we're making hay whenever the weather gives us three dry days. Our son Luke comes up most afternoons after his shift driving for the haulage firm.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's ours, and that it'll be Luke's. My father-in-law planted the shelter belt behind the house, and now I sit under it with my flask at ten o'clock. What wears me out is the forms. Every year there's more of them from people who've never stood in a wet field in their lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, there you are then. I could have told them that and saved everyone a lot of fuss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that real work is done with your hands and your head, not a computer. I'd say it after church to anyone who'd listen. I don't go online, so they'd have to hear it from me in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Highcroft carries on as it is, and Luke takes it over in his own time. That's all I've ever wanted. Nothing in that picture stands in the way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as always. Lambing in March, hay in July, the cattle sold in the autumn. We'd keep a few months' money in the bank like we do, and I'd keep trying to get Luke to come up full-time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit satisfied, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said satisfied. Who would you be satisfied about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The young man from the farming advice service who told us we'd be left behind. He came in a shiny car and wouldn't take his shoes off in my kitchen. I'd quite like to see his face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it take for Luke to come up full-time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, mostly. The farm can't pay two wages yet, so he drives to make ends meet. If the lamb price held a few good years, we'd have him home, and that's my prayer most Sundays.

S0.say: I'd say real work is done with your hands and your head, not a computer. I'd say it after church to anyone listening, because I don't go online.
S0.think: It means the family farm carries on and our son takes it over in his own time. Nothing in that picture stands in the way of what I've always wanted.
S0.do: Keeps the farming year as always, with lambing, hay and the autumn cattle sale. Keeps a few months' money in the bank and keeps encouraging her son to farm full-time.
S0.quote: He came in a shiny car and wouldn't take his shoes off in my kitchen. I'd quite like to see his face.
S0.fieldNote: Hana is rooted in four generations of family land and her whole outlook points at handing it to her son. Her distrust is aimed at outsiders who make rules without farming. She takes real pleasure in the idea of the experts being wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hm. That's more like what Luke says is coming. He watches the videos of the robot tractors on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let the big farms have their robots, the family farm will carry on the way it always has. I'd say it at the mart and at church. People round here would agree with me, most of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry it would push the prices down, because the big farms with robots can sell cheaper. That squeezes us, and it's harder to get Luke home. But I don't think it would change the work itself on a hill farm like ours, the robots can't manage the steep ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as we are, and tighten our belts a bit, no new quad, make the old one last. I wouldn't buy any of the new kit. I'd wait and see what it did to the lamb price before deciding anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, underneath. A sort of cold draught you can't find the source of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't manage the steep ground. How sure are you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sure enough for now. I've seen machines slide off our top field, and that was a tractor with a man in it. Mind, Luke says the new ones are cleverer, and he's usually right about machines, which annoys me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the prices did drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big companies that buy up the land and the government that lets them. And the supermarkets, who've always wanted food for nothing. Not the robots, they're just tools, it's who owns them.

S1.say: I'd say let the big farms have their robots, because the family farm will carry on as it always has. I'd say it at the mart and at church, where most would agree.
S1.think: I worry that big robot farms would sell cheaper and squeeze our prices, making it harder to bring our son home. I don't think robots could manage the steep ground on a hill farm like ours.
S1.do: Keeps going as before and tightens the belt by making the old quad bike last. Buys no new kit and waits to see what happens to the lamb price before deciding anything else.
S1.feel: Uneasy underneath, like a cold draught she can't trace.
S1.quote: Not the robots, they're just tools, it's who owns them.
S1.fieldNote: Hana's comfort rests on the hill being too steep for machines, though she admits her son knows better. She blames big companies, government and supermarkets, but not the technology itself. Her plans are to hold firm and spend less, with no new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Lord. That's not long at all. That's Luke's whole future gone before he's even started it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and that people in power let it happen because they never cared for country folk. I'd say it at church, at the mart, and to our representative if he ever came up the hill. I wouldn't be holding a sign, that's not our way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the farm wouldn't pay any more, not with robot farms selling lamb for next to nothing. Martin and I could live on it for a bit, we own it, we've a few months saved. But there'd be nothing for Luke to come home to, and that's what would break me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything we don't need, straight away, and keep the stock going as long as we could. I'd not sell the land, not to a company, not for any money. We'd lean on family, Luke and his sister, and the chapel folk, the way we always have, before I'd take a handout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in my stomach. I'd pray a lot, I know that much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luke when it became clear?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the land's still his, whatever it's worth, and it'll be here when things settle. I'd try not to cry in front of him. He'd go quiet, he does that, like his dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd not take a handout. If help came from the government, would you really refuse it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well. If it came to keeping the farm or not, I'd take it, I suppose, and feel ashamed. I'd want it to be something we work for, not a cheque for sitting still. But I wouldn't let my pride lose Highcroft.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong and that people in power let it happen because they never cared for country folk. I'd say it at church, at the mart and to our representative, but I wouldn't hold a sign.
S2.think: The farm wouldn't pay with robot farms selling lamb for next to nothing, though we own it and could live on it for a while. There'd be nothing for our son to come home to, and that would break me.
S2.do: Cuts all spending that isn't needed and keeps the stock as long as possible. Refuses to sell the land at any price and leans on her children and the chapel community, accepting government help only if it means keeping the farm.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick in her stomach, praying a lot.
S2.quote: If it came to keeping the farm or not, I'd take it, I suppose, and feel ashamed.
S2.fieldNote: The fast scenario threatens what Hana cares about most: passing the farm to her son. Her first reflex is family and chapel, not the state, but when pressed she admitted she'd accept help to save the land. The tension between pride and the farm was the most honest moment of the interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit better. Still fast, but you'd see it coming down the lane.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, that it's not right, but I'd also say families should start planning now. Get the young ones into the farm properly, while there's time. That's what I'd say at church and at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to get the farm into Luke's name and get him settled. If the worst comes, at least it's his land, and he can decide. Martin and I would be sixty-three and could step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd see the solicitor and start putting Highcroft into Luke's name, a bit at a time. I'd ask him to come up three days a week instead of afternoons, even if the farm can only pay him a little. And we'd save what we can, maybe give up the trip to my sister's in the spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do. I'm better with something to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luke's sister about putting the farm in his name?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Megan's a nurse in the city, she's never wanted the farm. I'd sit her down and explain it, and make sure she's looked after in the will some other way. She'd understand, she's a good girl, but I'd want her told face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you look at any of the new machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Luke might, and if it's his farm, that's his business. I'd tell him to only buy what he's seen work on a hill like ours, not on the flat.

S3.say: I'd say it's not right, but families should start planning now and get the young ones into the farm properly. I'd say that at church and at the young farmers' club.
S3.think: Five years is enough to put the farm in our son's name and get him settled. If the worst comes it's his land and his decision, and we could step back at sixty-three.
S3.do: Sees the solicitor this winter to start moving the farm into her son's name. Asks him to come up three days a week even on small pay, and saves by giving up a spring visit to her sister.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadied by having something to do.
S3.quote: Still fast, but you'd see it coming down the lane.
S3.fieldNote: With five years, Hana's answer is family succession: put the land in her son's name early. She would still never use the new machines herself and leaves that choice to him. She was careful to think about her daughter's fairness too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Luke would be forty-four. That's a long time in farming, but not long in the life of a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it right, so let's not lose our heads. Families, churches and villages need to look after each other, like we always did. I'd say that and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, for Martin and me, it's all right. We'd hand over in five years or so, as we'd planned. It's Luke who'd have to face it, and I'd want him ready for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd carry on farming and start the handover in a few years, not rushed. I'd want Luke to do one of the apprenticeship courses at the college, so he knows whatever's coming, not me. And I'd keep saving for when we step back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for Luke. For myself, I'd be calm enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd want Luke to learn about the new machines, but you won't. Why the difference?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's his life, not mine. I'm fifty-eight and I've done my learning. He's got thirty more years on that hill, and he needs whatever it takes to keep it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you hope the farm looks like in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheep on the top, cows on the bottom, Luke's children on the gate. Maybe a robot or two in the shed if he wants them. But a family still living in the house, that's the thing.

S4.say: I'd say there's time to do it right, so let's not lose our heads. Families, churches and villages need to look after each other as they always did.
S4.think: For my husband and me it's all right, because we'd hand over in about five years as planned. It's our son who would face it, and I'd want him ready.
S4.do: Carries on farming and starts an unhurried handover in a few years. Wants her son to take an apprenticeship course at the agricultural college on the new machines, and keeps saving for stepping back.
S4.feel: Uneasy for her son, calm enough for herself.
S4.quote: Sheep on the top, cows on the bottom, Luke's children on the gate.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years takes the pressure off Hana herself and puts it on her son, whom she wants trained for the change she refuses. She is clear about the difference: it's his life, not hers. Her hope for the farm is simple and centred on a family in the house.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Luke would lose the farm before he ever had it. What would help is keeping the big companies off family land, and help that's tied to working, like paying farmers to keep the hills grazed and the walls up. Not a cheque for doing nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the walls. Martin's grandfather built half the dry-stone walls on Highcroft by hand. A robot can do lots of things, I'm told, but somebody has to want those walls to still be standing.

headlineQuote: That's a long time in farming, but not long in the life of a farm.
portrait: Hana Moreau is a 58-year-old hill farmer who runs sheep, a few suckler cows, oats and hay on her husband's four-generation family farm. She has never used AI, gets her views across at church and the mart, and distrusts officials and big companies more than machines. Everything she says turns on handing the farm to her son Luke, who drives for a haulage firm to make ends meet. The two-year scenario alarms her because there'd be nothing for him to come home to, and she admits she'd accept help to keep the land. With five or ten years she plans an early handover and wants Luke trained for the change she won't make herself.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because her son would lose the farm before he ever had it.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping big companies off family land, and support tied to work, such as paying farmers to keep the hills grazed and the walls up, rather than a cheque for doing nothing.
